query: Refractory high-entropy alloys are promising structural materials, but achieving a strong combination of strength and plasticity remains important. What single intervention could improve this strength–plasticity combination? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, its expected mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an appropriate reference alloy, the conditions under which it should hold, supporting evidence from prior studies, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small, controlled amount of titanium to a refractory high‐entropy alloy (e.g., NbMoTaW) will improve its strength–plasticity combination by enhancing grain boundary cohesion and promoting more uniformly distributed plastic deformation.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high‐entropy alloy such as NbMoTaW that exhibits high yield strength but is limited in ductility due to brittle behavior and weak grain boundary cohesion.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor Ti addition into the alloy composition.
generation.conditions: The modification is evaluated under standard room‐temperature and high-temperature mechanical testing conditions using alloys processed under comparable thermo‐mechanical histories.
generation.structural_mediator: Improved grain boundary cohesion and possible promotion of nano‐twinning or a modified local atomic environment that delays the onset of intergranular fracture.
generation.mechanism: Titanium atoms segregate to grain boundaries and affect local bonding, thereby reducing the tendency for brittle intergranular failure while allowing for more homogeneous plastic deformation. This may also favor the activation of beneficial deformation mechanisms (such as nano-twinning) that contribute simultaneously to strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline NbMoTaW alloy without Ti, the Ti-enhanced alloy is expected to exhibit an increase in plastic strain (e.g., improvement on the order of ~10–15% in ductility) while maintaining or slightly improving the yield strength.
generation.baseline: The unmodified refractory HEA (e.g., NbMoTaW alloy) without titanium addition.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected only when Ti is added in a limited amount that does not induce formation of deleterious secondary phases; the mechanism may differ at very low temperatures (where martensitic transformations might dominate) compared to room and moderately elevated temperatures.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement and the optimal Ti concentration remain to be determined, and influences from processing conditions or slight compositional variations could affect the outcome.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of alloys: (1) baseline NbMoTaW and (2) NbMoTaW with a small, controlled addition of Ti, keeping processing parameters identical. Perform tensile tests at both room and elevated temperatures, and carry out microstructural characterizations (e.g., EBSD, TEM) focusing on grain boundary integrity and potential twin formation.
measurements: Observation of grain boundary cohesion and nano-twinning via microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti-added alloy does not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement (e.g., at least a ~10–15% increase in ductility or equivalent plastic strain) while retaining comparable or improved yield strength relative to the baseline, or if deleterious secondary phases form that lower the mechanical performance, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: With the development of high-temperature metallic materials, Ni-based superalloys have been unable to meet the requirements of aerospace engines. It is urgent to find a new high-performance alloy to replace the Ni-based superalloy []. Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) based on refractory elements with superior high-temperature mechanical properties have recently attracted intensive research attention, which are regarded as promising candidates for high-temperature structural materials [,,]. However, their inferior plasticity along with high ductile–brittle transition temperature and high density seriously limits their aerospace applications, where the requirements are mainly focus on the deformability and high specific strength of alloys.

One of the most promising and progressive fields in modern material science is high-entropy alloys (HEAs). The first to propose HEAs’ concept was J.W. Yeh [], but since then, it has changed rather significantly, especially during the last few years []. Due to their extremely high mechanical and physical properties, refractory HEAs are classified as a separate group of materials. Such alloying compositions mainly include elements from the IV, V, and VI columns of the periodic table with some additions of Al, Si, Ni, or Co []. First high-entropy equiatomic compositions based on refractory elements, such as NbMoTaW and NbMoTaWV, were obtained in prior research [,]. It was found that the alloys possess higher mechanical properties at higher temperatures in comparison to conventional superalloys, such as Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 []. It was also determined that the addition of V increases the hardness significantly (up to 11.4 GPa at 1150 °C) [] and yield strength σ0.2 from 1058 MPa to 1246 MPa [].
